grant.title: Better Border for a Better America University Transportation Center (B3A UTC)
grant.abstract: The William and Barbara Leonard Transportation Center at California State University at San Bernardino (lead), in collaboration with the Texas A&M Transportation Institute of the Texas A&M University System, the Arizona State University, the New Mexico State University, the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, the San Bernardino Valley College, and the Dona Ana Community College, is pleased to submit this proposal to create a Tier 1 University Transportation Center (UTC) addressing the statutory research priority of “improving mobility of people and goods.” The proposed Better Border for a Better America (B3A) UTC focuses on enhancing the efficient mobility of people and goods across the U.S.-Mexico border. The unique contribution of the B3A UTC’s research agenda is that it addresses the mobility challenges of people and goods across the southern border - critical for the country’s economic prosperity - while addressing the challenges that growing trade imposes on U.S. border communities. This is a complex problem that has not been sufficiently addressed in transportation research. The complexity of improving the mobility of people and goods is compounded in an international border environment by border regulations, the international jurisdictions involved, and the social and cultural dimensions. It requires not only a multi- disciplinary approach, but also a deep understanding of the challenges and the border communities that are impacted, as well as the importance of trade to the U.S., Mexico, border states, and local economies. The focus on improving mobility across the U.S.-Mexico border is particularly timely, given its national importance from an economic, national security, and justice perspective. In 2021, almost $1.5 billion in goods traded with Mexico crossed the U.S-Mexico border each day by truck or rail. Similarly, in 2021, 341,095 people crossed the border per day as pedestrians or in passenger vehicles. This growth is expected to continue with the signing of the 2020 U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement and the reconfiguration of global supply chains resulting in nearshoring and friend-shoring. There are several research questions that arise in the context of investing in and modernizing border infrastructure to enhance the efficient cross-border mobility of travelers and goods. Growing trade presents serious challenges to U.S. border communities, which are among the poorest in the nation and have for years borne the brunt of the negative impacts of international trade (e.g., traffic congestion and pollution). The B3A UTC will focus on exploring infrastructure, operational, technology, and policy/regulatory initiatives to prepare the border for the demands of the future, while recognizing the justice/equity, economic, global competitiveness, workforce development, and environmental (including resiliency and sustainability) impacts. In doing this, the B3A UTC will address several key challenges identified by U.S. DOT under the research priority areas, including freight logistics, data, and workforce; transportation equity; demand management; operations; environmental justice; resilience; and supply chain. The B3A UTC will also consider various candidate technologies identified by U.S. DOT in addressing these challenges, such as: vehicle-to-infrastructure, vehicle-to-pedestrian, vehicle-to-everything; simulation and modeling; artificial intelligence and machine learning; and community engagement. More specifically, the B3A UTC will explore the following focus areas: Infrastructure capacity solutions , such as heavy weight corridors that serve the international crossings and reduce the need for Mexican carriers to unload trucks before crossing the U.S.-Mexico border; Modernization and new technologies to help increase throughput on existing infrastructure, such as biometric and x-ray machines that remove the need for interaction with customs officials, smart border technologies, and new and emerging technologies to future-proof U.S.-Mexico cross-border transportation infrastructure; Operational Improvements of crossing and transportation corridors serving crossings to enhance capacity usage, such as unified cargo inspections and dynamic message signs to route traffic to less congested crossings; and New policy/ regulatory paradigms to improve cross-border governance and operations in the 21st century, as well as to overcome barriers to efficient cross-border movement, such as addressing the requirement for trains to change crews at the U.S.-Mexico border.These focus areas will be explored through the lenses of: justice/ equity - ensuring the research contributes to a more just outcome by promoting equity and equitable access for border communities to cross-border transportation services and to trade opportunities while mitigating impacts on disadvantaged and minority communities. economic impacts - ensuring the research considers the economic development/growth opportunities and impacts on border communities. climate, sustainability, and resiliency - ensuring the research contributes to a more resilient and sustainable U.S.-Mexico border transportation system, as well as mitigating the environmental impacts of increased cross-border travel and trade, such as increased criteria pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions. global competitiveness - ensuring the research addresses supply chain efficiencies, redundancies, and overall global competitiveness. workforce development - ensuring the research promotes training of border residents and access to higher paying jobs. By exploring these four focus areas through these five lenses, the B3A UTC will contribute to improving cross-border mobility while addressing the potential impacts on border communities to ensure an equitable sharing of the benefits and opportunities associated with increased trade. This holistic approach addresses the U.S. DOT’s strategic objectives of economic strength and global competitiveness, equity, climate and sustainability, and transformation.

grant.title: Improving Undergraduate STEM Education by Changing Institutional Culture
grant.sponsor: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
grant.abstract: Contextualization Families in the Rio Grande Valley, like other minority groups, have historically been exploited, dominated, acculturated, subjugated, and marginalized socially, culturally, linguistically and educationally (Valencia, 2010). Such historical realities have kept Hispanic families, and other groups underrepresented in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) from finding a true sense of belonging, even after living in the region(s) for generations. The creation of The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), founded with values and beliefs that are culturally responsive to the communities it serves, presents greater opportunities for Hispanic families and communities and other minorities underrepresented in higher education, especially in STEM disciplines (e.g., first generation, females, international, transfer, commuting, and non-English speaking). Since its establishment in 2015, UTRGV has made significant leaps in research, teaching, and service. Student success has been at its center for countless initiatives. Even though several initiatives have had significant gains in desired academic and non-academic outcomes, none has had a broader impact than the current NSF funded initiative HSI Institutional Transformation Project: Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Through Family-Centered Pedagogy (award number 2122875). This program impacted over 1,200 undergraduate students enrolled in Physics, Chemistry, and Mathematics courses in the 2022-2023 academic year. We observed increased engagement and participation from STEM undergraduate students, with the support of over 300 families from underrepresented communities in the RGV. Moreover, in a survey conducted at the end of the semester symposium, most students, their families, AVE Frontera family leaders, and STEM faculty reported experiencing a strong sense of belonging with ownership and pride. They noted that this was an event where families from the local community came together to support STEM students in a family-friendly, family-integrated learning environment at UTRGV. The preliminary data observed at UTRGV suggests that the proposed project has the potential to shed new light to “sense of belonging with ownership and pride” and Institutional Social Responsibility (Salinas, 2018) among Hispanic students, families and other underrepresented communities in STEM. Theoretical Framework Our theoretical framework encompasses: 1) a novel Family-Centered Theory of Change that addresses diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI); and 2) an intersectionality lens used to guide and assess the transformational impact on teaching and learning, curricula, student success, assessment, and pedagogical practices in undergraduate physics, mathematics, and chemistry courses. The proposed project benefits from the relational partnership between leaders from an institution of higher education, UTRGV, and leaders from a community-based organization, AVE Frontera. AVE (A Vehicle of Engagement) Frontera is a grassroots advocacy group that serves as a vehicle of engagement that is family-centered, instills cultural pride and awareness amongst its members, and fulfills their physical, emotional, social, spiritual, and intellectual needs. The Family-Centered Model brings stakeholders in a process of sustainable knowledge co-production (Norström et al., 2020) allowing students, families from the community, faculty, and researchers to co-develop pedagogical and research practices impacting engaged student learning and institutional culture change. The goal of the proposed project is twofold: 1) to create a sustainable institutional culture of mentorship in STEM research; and 2) to create a sustainable institutional culture of engaged student learning in STEM. Family-Centered Project Activities Activities for Goal 1 Project efforts will go towards creating a sustainable institutional culture of mentorship in STEM Research. The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) was founded in 2015, through the merger of the two legacy institutions: University of Texas Pan American and University of Texas Brownsville (both legacy institutions serving the Rio Grande Valley Region [RGV] of South Texas), as a Doctoral/Professional University and has since worked towards the goal of becoming an R1 University. In 2019 UTRGV went from a Doctoral/Professional University to becoming an R2 University and continues to aim towards becoming an R1 university. Through the Family-Centered Model, we plan to foster a culture of mentorship in STEM Research that will strengthen STEM education at UTRGV as well as support UTRGV’s goal of becoming an R1 institution. The STEM faculty participating in the undergraduate research mentoring will: Mentor/train the undergraduate students in research skills;Generate family-friendly environments where students’ family members arewelcomed to participate in research activity discussions; Be open to exploring valid and reasonable options of incorporating interestedstudents’ family members into the research endeavor; As PI submit and develop a research proposal by the end of the year;The submitted proposal will include active collaboration of the participatingundergraduate students and their families, including proposal writing. Activities for Goal #2 Project efforts will also go towards creating a sustainable institutional culture of engaged student learning in STEM. We will also have one convocation (mini-conference) per semester where participating faculty, students, and students’ families can meet, share experiences and present results. The convocations will be open to culturally relevant, community-engaged, and/or family-centered pedagogy scholars, and to all interested students (goal is 75-100 participants). We will also have one summer student-workshop per year for the participating students to explore future graduate studies and work options, to help students prepare for graduate school applications, and to prepare CVs for private sector job applications. By establishing undergraduate student/faculty teams, faculty will be encouraged to incorporate undergraduate students to research endeavor nurturing an engaged learning environment. By fostering a family-friendly environment, the undergraduate student will be more motivated to pursue research at undergraduate levels and additionally it also produces a stronger support from the families for the student to pursue a STEM research career, that in turn should increase student retention rates in STEM. The grant-preparing experience gained by the undergraduate student will also prepare the student for future graduate studies and beyond. Further, with a fraction of the total proposal submitted approved, this will motivate faculty to continue incorporating undergraduate students in research efforts as well gain the support of Departmental and College administration for these efforts leading to sustainability. The Research and Mentoring effort of this project will directly impact fourteen STEM faculty and twenty-eight STEM students. Of course, in nurturing a sustainable culture of mentorship in STEM Research that actively incorporates undergraduate students, we expect the impact to be much larger (60 STEM faculty, 200 students) over the duration of the project, supporting our colleges and university efforts towards becoming an R1 institution.

grant.abstract: Groundbreaking advances in advanced manufacturing processes and smart technologies for cyber-physical systems are driving revolutions in materials/structures design and synthesis, providing innovation opportunities that transform a broader spectrum of military systems where advanced performance and protection at extreme conditions are expected. The objective of this request is to support a stream of ongoing research projects and two national consortia led by the PI team, through which 4 minority institutions are supported. Specifically, this requested major equipment supports UTRGV DoD Consortium for Innovation Driven Research Education for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D, www.idream4d.org) funded by DoD ($3.9 million, 2020-2024). The consortium is composed of five higher education institution members with three minority-serving institutions (UTRGV, UTSA, and Virginia State University), two national labs (Army Research Lab, Oak Ridge National Lab), members from defense industry, local high schools, and community colleges. The requested metal additive manufacturing machine facilitates the goals of the consortium to 1) advance research in material engineering through additive manufacturing (AM) and AI; 2) sustain an innovation-driven manufacturing education ecosystem to prepare future scientists and engineers who lead U.S. defense manufacturing innovation; and 3) expose and recruit future STEM talents through high school summer manufacturing innovation camps , and regional defense expos/exhibitions planned in 5 regions the consortium serves with a total population of 20 million, most of which are from underrepresented minority groups. UTRVG, a multi-campus and the nation’s second-largest Hispanic-serving institute (HSI) has a record high total enrollment of 32,618 in Fall 2020, of whom 89.4% are Hispanic. The requested equipment is critical to the goal of increasing participation of underrepresented minorities in all STEM programs and specifically in advanced materials and manufacturing while broadening and enhancing UTRGV’s core priority of student success through engaged learning, research, and creative works that will transform the Rio Grande Valley, the Americas, and beyond. The requested Metal Additive Manufacturing Equipment supports funded research projects and education programs organized in three levels, with the participation of minority students and faculty at UTRGV: 1) Advanced material synthesis and additive manufacturing science; 2) Materials/structure design enabled by AM and Artificial Intelligence (AI); and 3) Military devices and components enabled by AM and AI. Since 2019, the team has engaged more than 652 undergraduate students in the defense manufacturing education program, supported more than 95 students in funded research and industry projects, and exposed 1300 high school students to advanced defense manufacturing technologies though defense expos , summer camps, and invited talks provided by DoD. The team at UTRGV was recenlty selected by DOE/NNSA and NSF for awards of two large grants ($9 million total) to prepare STEM talents and to advance research at UTRGV, leveraging AM for energy production and critical infrastructures. Currently, the team only has limited access to a Renishaw AM 400 machine located in LA, California, through a collaboration arrangement, which is no longer sufficient to support the research and education programs at UTRGV. The pandemic has additionally caused serious logistic challenges to all operations at every facet. Direct access to modern metal additive manufacturing machines is in desperate need to support a stream of funded projects, support student learning in STEM, and support impactful outreach programs the team offers.

grant.abstract: In-situ alloying is a highly desired capability by the metal Additive Manufacturing (AM) industry. Research in in-situ alloying could realize the full potential of metal additive manufacturing, supporting material and structure innovation for automobile, energy, and space applications. The preliminary work at University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) demonstrates the possibility of in-situ direct alloying based on elemental metal particles using a Selected Laser Melting AM machine. Despite the low flowability of particles and insufficient diffusion, our work demonstrated the potential of in-situ alloying of configurable binary, ternary, and high entropy alloys (HEAs) directly from multiple elemental metals, using laser and multi-energy sources to control the melting-alloying-solidification cycles involved in the process. However, as with any alloying process, complete diffusion of metal atoms is necessary for the formation of random solid solution, the signature structure of any HEA. In the meantime, the preliminary work at Leibniz Universität Hannover (LUH) reveals that the diffusion of different elements is significantly increased by ultrasound vibration. It is also revealed that, within the vibration environment, metals are melted at a lower temperature than their melting point and grains can be refined. The collaboration between UTRGV and LUH provides a unique opportunity to accelerate and control effective diffusion required in processing multi-materials in a single step . In this project, the fundamental mechanisms involved in laser-based in-situ alloying and fusing of multi-elements and multi-materials assisted by ultrasound vibration will be systematically investigated. The team will first investigate the melting, diffusion and solidification of Al-Fe binary systems under ultrasonic vibration, based on a single hatch melt pool. The expected scientific findings include the process behaviors detected using high-speed observations and real-time temperature measurements of laser melt pool. The diffusion behaviors and the resulting material structures across scales will be observed by EDX and XRD. The observed material melting/diffusion/solidification behaviors and resulting material structures created in a single hatch melt pool will allow the team to develop a fundamental process/material behavior relationship considering both laser and ultrasonic process parameters. Multi-hatch strategies will be explored to fabricate samples, which will be studied for mechanical and physical property testing. A process-material-structure property relationship model will then be developed to support future industry adoption of the in-situ alloying based additive processes.

grant.abstract: Overview: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes to establish the “CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS).” The Center’s mission is to advance and transform the much-needed research and education at the nexus of automation, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI), as integral parts of the “NSF’s 10 Big Ideas,” anticipating the revolutionary cyber-physical infrastructure systems (CIS). Three Colleges of Engineering, Sciences, and Education at UTRGV in collaboration with the Universities of Illinois (at Urbana-Champaign and at Chicago) and California (Riverside) will pursue multidisciplinary research on CIS, aiming to: (i) transfer technology to various transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and construction industries; and (ii) prepare a minority STEM workforce to drive future CIS-based communities. The Center envisions a portfolio of three research subprojects on automation, sensors, and AI that bridges diverse STEM disciplines. A holistic, multi-level approach is adopted to address CIS planning, design, and operation. While each subproject constitutes a unique element, their synergy ensures the CIS integrity. Subproject 1 pushes the frontiers of knowledge in future transportation infrastructure, which will be transformed by autonomous vehicles (AVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), in six directions: (i) at the planning level, public acceptance and policy issues of (U)AV; (ii-iv) at the design level, computer vision, automatic navigation, and model/field-based testing of the designed capabilities; and (v, vi) at the operation level, human-(U)AV interactions and network-wide inter-(U)AV interactions. Subproject 2 designs and embeds sensors in CIS for two purposes. First, (U)AV sensors help perform automated tasks. Second, sensors in civil infrastructure and (U)AVs monitor infrastructure health. Three research areas are defined: (i, ii) at the design level, computational simulation, synthesis, and 3D printing of sensor materials and UAV structures, and (iii) at the operation level, cost-effective decision-making to upkeep infrastructure health using sensor data. Since (U)AVs and sensors will inherently generate big data, Subproject 3 will synchronously work with subprojects 1 and 2 to: (i) develop AI solutions for big data management, and (ii) develop AI algorithms for big data analytics and decision making in the design and operation of (U)AVs and infrastructure. UTRGV is the nation’s second largest Hispanic-Serving Institute (HIS) located in South Texas with an established record of preparing underrepresented minority students for STEM careers. grant.abstract: The objective of this proposal is to acquire a state of the art surface characterization system including nano-indentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research projects and education programs in areas of interest to DoD at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The proposed system will include cutting-edge features needed to characterize a broad range of materials and provide the capability to investigate mechanical, tribological and other physical properties at nanostructured scales for materials that are too thin to be tested using conventional methods. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The acquisition of the proposed equipment will allow the surface characterization of the materials created by the sputtering system, which will immediately benefit research and educational projects in areas of interest to DoD. These projects include the following: (1) High temperature characterization of novel thermal barrier coatings created by PVD. Encompassing the development of novel PVD protective thermal barrier coatings TBC for gas turbine engines and the analytical methods to study their mechanical properties and adhesion to turbine blade materials at elevated temperatures. (2) Cost-effective CIGS thin films for novel solar power technology, encompassing the development of thin film solar cell like Copper Indium Gallium Di-Selenide (CIGS) with an optimized design considering the efficiency and cost effectiveness, to be used for space and satellite applications. grant.abstract: The SEPA Biomedical @ the Rio Grande Valley Project will take multi-faceted approach to research educational interventions with the ultimate goal of broadening biomedical research participation of underrepresented Hispanic students from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas on the U.S./Mexican Border. This region of Texas has the highest poverty rate in the United States and a population that is over 90% Hispanic. Most high school teachers are not prepared to teach biomedical curriculum nor the training and skills to carry out biomedical research. As a result, students are not exposed to biomedical research experiences that would help them to be prepared for pursuing a STEM or STEM related undergraduate degree. This problem is magnified for underrepresented populations who lack access to high quality, equitable education opportunities. This proposal seeks to address this problem by (1) providing summer research experiences for high school teachers. High school teachers will gain biomedical research content and knowledge through these paid summer research experiences. (Sub Aim 1 of Specific Aim 1). Participant high school teachers will also work with UTRGV education faculty to develop biomedical experiential learning modules during their summer internships to incorporate into their high school teaching (Sub Aim 2 of Specific Aim 1) in order to increase biomedical content and skills for high school students. (2) Specific Aim 2 will have under-represented high school students perform biomedical research side-by-side with high school teachers during the summer, implementing an educative learning model to increase biomedical research content, knowledge and enthusiasm for these students. (3) Specific Aim 3 will provide high school students with biomedical experiential learning using a university mobile science laboratory. Hypothesis: mobile laboratory activities will have a positive impact on high school students’ attitudes toward STEM careers. Our short-term goal is to excite students about careers in biomedical science and to strengthen ties between area schools and UTRGV. Our midterm goal is to increase educational attainment in STEM to ultimately increase representation of Hispanics in the biomedical science workforce. Educational research will focus on a large number of at-risk students in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, which will enable ultimately crafting programs that succeed at increasing educational equity for these students and representation in biomedical science careers.

grant.title: Advanced Manufacturing
grant.abstract: Titanium and Nickel-based alloys have seen increased utilization in military and aerospace applications because of a combination of high specific strength, toughness, corrosion resistance, elevated-temperature performance and compatibility with polymer composite materials. These material properties are essential requirements for certain critical parts such as wing supports and jet engine components. For decades, the high-speed machining of these alloys has created considerable interest to researchers, tool manufacturers and end users because titanium alloys are difficult to machine due to their inherent low thermal conductivity and higher chemical reactivity with other materials at elevated temperatures. It has been observed that plastic deformation and dissolution wear are two major detrimental mechanisms in high-speed machining of titanium alloys which contribute to tool failure. In addition, thermal cycling due to the serration process at the tool-workpiece interface, affects the tool life significantly. I plan to conduct research on “High Speed Machining of Titanium Alloys”. The designed experiments will be conducted on a milling machine using different type of coated cutting inserts. The output parameters such as cutting forces, tool-wear/life, surface finish will be measured to compare the performance of various coated tools during the milling operation. The process optimization will be conducted based on the results.

grant.title: CAREER PROPOSAL: Analysis and Decision Support for National Security Sensitive Queueing Systems – A U.S. Commercial Border Crossing Tool
grant.abstract: Project Summary This integrated research and education project proposes a multi-tier solution to a stochastic, non-stationary, and terminating queuing system that is visible in the congestion of the commercial border crossing process at the United States (U.S.) border. This proposal focuses on a multiple tier approach to improve this system by utilizing technical queueing theory aspects on truck lines, simulation modeling, and data analytics to influence human decision behavior, while integrating educational components to facilitate the dissemination of information to the multinational community and region, without affecting the security procedures or the costs at the Ports of Entry (POE). Additional benefits that can be realized include congestion reduction on both sides of the border, improved utilization of major facilities and infrastructure, and reduced pollution generated by the idling of commercial trucks. According to the U.S. Department of Transportation (US DOT, 2016), over 11 million commercial trucks came into the U.S. in 2015, not including private vehicles and pedestrian traffic, through one of over 100 major border POEs. At the Southern U.S. border over 5.5 million commercial trucks entered the country through the over 20 POEs (BTS, 2016). However, securing our southwest border from terrorist interventions, undocumented immigrants, and the illegal flow of drugs and guns has dominated the ability to efficiently and effectively process people, goods and traffic. Increasing security and inspection requirements are seriously affecting transit times. Each POE is configured as a multi-commodity, prioritized queueing network which rarely, if ever, operates in steady-state. Therefore, the challenge is to balance 1) a reduction of wait time and its variance; 2) effectively utilize resources and minimize cost of POE operations, and 3) the sustainment of a security levels through Agent training, inspection and detection. The intellectual merit of this proposal is based on using queueing theory and simulation on the border crossing process to implement methodologies that addresses port utilization and efficiency, which affects wait times, without increasing costs or affecting security procedures. An analytical model of a stochastic, non-stationary, and terminating queuing system is challenging because of the number of states in the system given the trucks at the POE. A simulation model, validated through the analytical model, will serve to implement and test throughput improvement methodologies that do not affect cost or security procedures. Improvements include the Dynamic Reallocation Methodology (DRM), lane availability policies, and the effect of influencing supply chain arrival data of commercial trucks. The second contribution addresses inspection (service) times under time-varying arrivals (demands). By developing secondary inspection policies, primary inspection time variance can be reduced. In the simulation model, a Markovian service time will be assumed first. However, prior work and field data suggest a general distribution that will be estimated using a Coxian k-phased approximation. The third contribution is the development of a mobile app that will serve as a decision support application for the general public. Current wait time sources are estimates at best. An application that utilizes historical data can influence companies and people to select alternatives to congested border crossing points, and improve efficiencies. The broader impact of this proposal applies to the international region that includes south Texas and northern Mexico. Improvements will benefit border communities economically and the general population through increased security. Finally, by incorporating into current educational efforts, new engineers and the general public can be educated to make better decisions.

grant.abstract: This proposal establishes the Center for Integrated Transportation Infrastructure 4.0 (CITI-4.0), a National University Transportation Center focusing on “Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure”. CITI 4.0 is a consortium of seven US higher education and research institutions that consolidate their expertise, facilities, resources, and institutional support to achieve the common goals of the center. The center addresses the challenges of the new era Intelligent Transportation System in ways never previously imagined by adapting the “Industry 4.0” principles to the integrated transportation infrastructure. CITI-4.0 introduces automation, cyber-physical fusion and information driven practices, enabled by real-time data communications among heterogeneous monitoring sensors and integrates the assessment, management and maintenance activities of the infrastructure, resources and operations across railways, roadways, and ports following a data-driven performance-based approach. Motives: North America’s demand for safe, affordable, and environmentally responsible transportation of people and goods by railway, roadway, and ports is projected to grow substantially in the years ahead. Asset managers are consistently challenged to improve the performance of the transportation network, optimize efficiency of operations and ensure safety by maximizing accessibility and reliability of the transportation infrastructure. Although accurate monitoring is a key enabler for effective operations and maintenance, the condition assessment is currently conducted based mainly on periodic, labor-intensive and time-consuming scheduled activities. The interpretation of the collected data and integration with operations is extensively dependent on the experience of the operators and other human factors. Each transportation mode relies typically on its own operations, infrastructure, and resources to meet the current network demand. These three elements are often loosely integrated within each mode, are rarely integrated across modes, and are not effectively engaged with the end users of the network. Topic Areas: The center activities cover the following non-exclusive topics: (1) Application of new materials and technologies; (2) Cyber and communications security; (3) Condition monitoring, remote sensing, and the use of GPS; (4) Asset and performance management through data accessibility, data security and analytical tools; Impacts: CITI-4.0 brings the infrastructure of the major transportation modes into the Industry 4.0 era as essential parts of the grand Intelligent Transportation System. The proposed CITI-4.0 research, education, workforce development, technology transfer, and diversity activities advance technology in transportation engineering and enable students and professionals from diverse socioeconomic groups throughout the country to develop the skills necessary to overcome the transportation challenges of the next era and create the next generation of worldwide leaders. This initiative benefits all stakeholders in the transportation industry, administration and legislation and sets the framework for addressing similar problems around the world.

Therefore, the challenge is to balance 1) a reduction of wait time and its variance; 2) effectively utilize resources and minimize cost of POE operations, and 3) the sustainment of a security levels through Agent training, inspection and detection. The intellectual merit of this proposal is based on using queueing theory and simulation on the border crossing process to implement methodologies that addresses port utilization and efficiency, which affects wait times, without increasing costs or affecting security procedures. An analytical model of a stochastic, non-stationary, and terminating queuing system is challenging because of the number of states in the system given the trucks at the POE. A simulation model, validated through the analytical model, will serve to implement and test throughput improvement methodologies that do not affect cost or security procedures. Improvements include the Dynamic Reallocation Methodology (DRM), lane availability policies, and the effect of influencing supply chain arrival data of commercial trucks. The second contribution addresses inspection (service) times under time-varying arrivals (demands). By developing secondary inspection policies, primary inspection time variance can be reduced. In the simulation model, a Markovian service time will be assumed first. However, prior work and field data suggest a general distribution that will be estimated using a Coxian k-phased approximation. The third contribution is the development of a mobile app that will serve as a decision support application for the general public. Current wait time sources are estimates at best. An application that utilizes historical data can influence companies and people to select alternatives to congested border crossing points, and improve efficiencies. The broader impact of this proposal applies to the international region that includes south Texas and northern Mexico. Improvements will benefit border communities economically and the general population through increased security. Finally, by incorporating into current educational efforts, new engineers and the general public can be educated to make better decisions.

grant.abstract: Narrative Project Description Spectroscopy can be used to detect explosives efficiently through the absorption response of organic materials in the mid-infrared range. A mid-infrared spectrometer typically consists of a broadband thermal emitter and broadband detector, external optics, as well as a Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR). All these components can be incorporated into a single chip, and this will provide the advantage or portability and low cost. Lin P. T. et al. (2014) have developed a mid-infrared spectrometer for on-chip chemical sensing using silicon/silicon dioxide wave guides. The on-chip device still requires a sufficient concentration of the chemical in order to detect it and separate the signature from the background noise. The goal of this research is to build microfluidic channels in the wave guides that can concentrate the airborne particles present in the air to a level that they are detectable by chip-based spectroscopy. 1. Design and simulation of nano-fluidic channel Detection of airborne particles require a deliberate design of flow passages for gas sampling. The flow of the fluid medium and the movement of the particles in it must be simulated using a computer fluid dynamics program. Micro- and nanofluidic devices are designed more commonly for liquid flow or multiphase flow applications. Microchannels are often classified as channels with a characteristic length (e.g. hydraulic diameter) of 10-200 μm, whereas nanochannels have hydraulic diameters under 0.1 μm (Kandlikar and Grande, 2003). In liquids, molecular mean free path is in sub-nanometer scale and therefore liquid flows in microchannels are treated with conventional fluid models. However, for gas flows in microfluidic channels, traditional fluid models based on continuum mechanics theories do not apply. Because the mean free path of air molecules at atmospheric conditions is about 70 μm, no-slip boundary conditions for larger channel flow do not apply to microchannels. Partial vacuum conditions that can occur in gas sampling flow passages further increase the molecular mean free path. For nanofluidic channels, the mean free path for gas molecules is significantly larger than the channel diameter. This means nanochannels should only be use in large numbers and short lengths, in order to attain a meaningful flow sampling. For gas flows with large Knudsen numbers (Kn = λ/L), traditional finite-volume or finite-difference method solvers for Navier-Stokes equations cannot be used as they are based on a continuum hypothesis. An appropriate simulation tool is the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method (Bird, 1994), which has been used for vacuum applications such as high altitude space crafts and laser ablation process. DSMC has also been used for some MEMS simulations. One of the existing DSMC software tools is dsmcFoam, which has been developed as a part of the open source CFD package OpenFoam by Scanlon et al. (2010). This tool can be applied to both 2D and 3D flows that can be either steady or unsteady. By conducting probabilistic simulations of a large number of particles and their interactions within the simulation domain, the flow phenomenon is captured as a statistical average. grant.title: GOALI: Study of Selective Laser Alloying of Elemental Metal Powders
grant.abstract: Overview: Selective laser alloying, an innovative process first attempted at PIs? lab, showed potential of advancing the scientific and engineering foundations in material processing. In this novel approach, instead of prealloyed powders, pure elemental powders are selectively melted by a laser beam, and then react into desired alloys at desired locations. This creates unique opportunities to transform material/structure/device design and fabrication with following advantages: 1) free forming with adjustable material composition/property along all three axes. 2) significantly reduced energy consumption in 3D laser processing utilizing energy released from the reaction process, 3) 3D forming of high melting point ceramic materials from elemental powders at much lower processing temperature, 4) creating micron-scale porous structures with controllable shape, size, and desired 3-dimensional spatial arrangements. While the concept of this process was successfully proved with patents pending by a team of students and faculty at PIs? lab (US Patent 6493-03100), our initial investigation also exposed fundamental research questions that must be addressed before it can spin off innovations in a stream of applications in both commercial and defense sectors. Targeted on these challenges/opportunities, an interdisciplinary team of experts from equipment manufacturers, application user (ARL), and academic researchers, will jointly investigate the important research questions aiming to understand the structure-property-processing relationships associated with the novel process. Specifically, the team will investigate the intrinsic heating-prereaction-alloying-melting-solidification process cycle at multi-spatial-temporal scales, so as to predict process behavior and property of the micro/meso/macro structures created. Special phenomena such as the speculated Kirkendall effect, Kirkendall porosity, and exothermic reaction between elemental powders at microscale will be investigated. PIs will also develop heat models to direct the experiments, eventually help better understanding of the structure-property-processing relationships, control of the process, and attaining desired structures and properties of fabricated products. Intellectual Merit: Currently, metal free-forming utilizing exothermic reaction between elemental powders has not been well addressed and studied in literature. Study of Kirkendall effects in a powder based binary system at micro scale can be another important contribution to the literature. The study will also advance knowledge about pore formation in the select laser alloying which can help understand the determining factors for the size, shape, and 3 dimensional spatial arrangement of the pore networks. This can eventually help the team to develop the process-property relationship for this novel process and for wider adoption in industry. Knowledge discovered in this research can be applied to processing of other multi-material metal powder systems. Broader Impacts: If succeeds, this research can spin off innovations in a stream of applications that require extremely hard materials with extremely high melting temperature, excellent heat conductivity, oxidation stability, resistance to mechanical erosion, and good electrical conductivity. This research could also create a transformative technology to significantly reduce energy consumption in laser processing and enable the fabrication of porous structured materials integrating with 3D free forming for applications in defense, medical, aerospace and oil industries. The research projects will provide exciting education and research opportunities for the graduate and undergraduate students at UTRGV. UTRGV is a major Hispanic serving institution; around 90% of its 30,000 enrolled students are Hispanic Americans. The team also has strong record in technology transfer and commercialization. Dr. Li and Xu are now participating in the NSF I-Corp program. Technologies develop in this research project will be eventually transferred or commercialized to benefit the communities and society at the regional and national levels.

grant.abstract: We propose to research the applications of virtual reality to maritime and port security. The potential applications of virtual reality (VR) hardware to increase maritime domain awareness and to enhance the response capabilities of homeland security practitioners are numerous. The proposed research project explores a range of applications, including but not limited to, the use of VR to visualize imaging sonar data collected from remotely operated vehicles (ROV’s). An example may include operations in which ROV’s are used to perform ship hull and pier piling inspections to search for parasitic devices. Through the visualization of what an ROV would see underwater and the 3-D experience of the VR, the ROV operators can enhance skills and better prepare themselves for conducting inspections in a range of underwater environments (e.g. cloudy water, rough currents, narrow and constrained spaces, etc.). VR environments created through this research, can also assist operators to assess the effectiveness of integrated sensors (e.g. positional sensors, imaging sensors and cameras used for underwater mapping) from the location and view point of an ROV. grant.abstract: The four counties in deep south Texas known as the Rio Grande Valley are home to one of the fastest growing populations and one of the fastest growing manufacturing sectors in the state of Texas and world. The region is known as the Rio Grande Valley because it is located on the northern banks of the Rio Grande River which serves as the international boundary between the United States and Mexico. The Rio Grande Valley is also home to the second largest federally certified Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI) of higher education in the United States, the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Approximately 90% of the more than 25,000 UTRGV students are Hispanic. The UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) has been recognized for the quality of its academic programs and the numerous partnerships and collaborations that its faculty have established with more than 100 entities in its service area including manufacturers, local governments, economic development councils, two year institutions of higher education and not-for-profit organizations. Through the provision of these industrial energy assessments the South Texas IAC has the potential of assisting manufacturers to save millions of dollars each year in energy and water management costs. The proposal to develop a South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (South Texas IAC) described herein is made possible because of a number of CECS engineering faculty who possess the requisite expertise and willingness to work with 20 UTRGV engineering students to carry out twenty industrial assessments per year. The faculty participating in the activities being proposed herein represent all of the departments in the CECS including electrical engineering, manufacturing and industrial engineering, civil engineering, and mechanical engineering. The diversity of faculty members’ areas of specialization and their various departmental affiliations in the CECS will provide students with an appreciation of the cross disciplinary nature of industrial energy assessments. Development and Characterization of Cold Spray Coatings for Aerospace and Defense Manufacturing
presentation.event: 16th North American Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management
presentation.abstract: Cold Spray is a type of thermal metal spraying which uses heated gas/air to propel metal powder onto the surface of a substrate to create a coating or repair damaged or corroded metal components. The powder feedstock materials are spherical gas atomized metal powders ranging in size from 20-50 microns in diameter for best results. Cold spray systems use low temperatures ranging from 200-900 °C compared to existing additive manufacturing methods which use much higher temperatures to melt metal. These lower heating temperatures only semi-melt the metal powder particles allowing for them to undergo plastic deformation as they are deposited onto the surface of the substrate. The main objective of this project is to develop and characterize cold spray coatings using aluminum, copper, and nickel powders deposited on different substrates varying processing parameters. As cold spray can be used in different coating applications with a wide range of different metals and alloys, coatings have an unlimited range in applications where rapid repair and high-quality coatings are needed. The ease of use of this technology has a promising future in aerospace and defense applications as it provides a low-cost solution in corrosion prevention and repair of damaged components.

presentation.title: INDIRECT ANALYSIS OF INJECTION MOLDING USING FLOW SIMULATION
presentation.abstract: The plastic injection molding process is widely used and of great importance for the manufacturing process production of plastic parts in many applications such as automotive, sports, electronics and many more endless applications. Injection molding process has many advantages, such as short production cycles, can be performed with many different types of materials, provides excellent surface of products and facilitates the molding of complicated shapes. However, in order to achieve benefits of injection molding process, proper design of mold is very critical. Often flow simulation software such as Moldlfow are widely used to optimize product design and process conditions for injection molding process. However, injection molding defect such as flash is not predictable since most flow simulation software does not provide as an option. Even properly designed mold can develop flash. Flash is caused by aging of mold, changes of resin and/or process conditions. Even though flash may not a major defect, it requires flash removal process and scrap rate increases during removal of flash process. In this research, production mold from Steel Case was chosen as a case study and flash was estimated by monitoring pressure at the point of flash. A least pressure condition was found and proved through test molding of sample at the optimum condition. Flash was effectively eliminated.

presentation.title: Static Mixer for Heat Transfer Enhancement for Mold Cooling Application
presentation.organization: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
presentation.abstract: Injection molding is the process by which a material is melted in a barrel and then it is injected through a nozzle in the mold cavity. When it cools down, the material solidifies into the shape of the cavity. Typical injection mold has cooling channels to maintain constant mold temperature during injection molding process. Even and constant temperature throughout the mold are very critical for a part quality and productivity. Conformal cooling improves the quality and productivity of injection molding process through the implementation of cooling channels that ``conform'' to the shape of the molded part. Recent years, the use of conformal cooling increases with advance of 3D printing technology such as Selective Laser Melting (SLM). Although it maximizes cooling, material and dimension limitations make SLM methods highly expensive. An alternative is the addition of static mixers in the molds with integrated cooling channels. A static mixer is a motionless mixing device that enhances heat transfer by producing improved flow mixing in the pipeline. In this study, the performance of the cooling channels will be evaluated with and without static mixers, by measuring temperature, pressure drop, and flow rate. The following question is addressed: Can a static mixer effectively enhance heat transfer for mold cooling application processes? This will provide insight on the development of design methods and guidelines that can be used to increase cooling efficiency at a lower cost.

presentation.title: Surface geometry modification for effective water spreading
presentation.organization: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
presentation.abstract: Liquid spreading on solid surfaces depend on the kind of materials (liquid, solid, and vapor) and the interface geometries. Many applications involving liquid deposition by spraying and condensation require deliberate management of liquid spreading over the surfaces. In this work water spreading on solid surfaces with geometrical patterns are observed by experiments in an environmental chamber, which is controlled for temperature and humidity. Water will be deposited to the surfaces through spraying and condensation on a Peltier cooling stage. An optical microscope camera is utilized to observe static and dynamic liquid spreading behavior during the tests. Various test samples of different surface wettability and geometrical modifications are created by 3d printing technique. There are numerous studies that uses chemical coatings for wettability modification providing an effective solution. But these conventional techniques have limited long term reliability when the surface is exposed to environmental contamination which degrades the wetting behavior over time. By adding geometrical features less than a millimeter in the length scale, sustained ``highways'' are created on the surfaces, which provide an effective method for liquid drainage path with long term reliability. A successful implementation will lead to increased efficiency of applications such as dehumidifiers, heating and cooling systems in buildings and power plants.
